Although no real evidence of a teratogenic effect exists,34 therapy has tended to be reserved for severe cases, and short-term use. Persistent vomiting and severe nausea may progress to hyperemesis gravidarum if adequate hydration cannot be maintained; the condition occurs in up to 1% of pregnan- cies.35 Management of hyperemesis includes hospitalisa- tion for intravenous fluid and electrolyte replacement, and this is usually sufficient. Routine thiamine supplementa- tion, by mouth if tolerated, otherwise parenterally, has been recommended to reduce the risk of Wernicke’s encephalopathy35,36 (p.1977), although there is some dis- sent from this view.37 If hyperemesis fails to respond to rehydration, antiemetics should be used; options include domperidone, phenothiazines, and antihistamines.35 It has been suggested that hyperemesis unresponsive to conven- tional therapy may respond to oral prednisolone or intrave- nous hydrocortisone.35 There have also been anecdotal re- ports of ondansetron being used successfully in life- threatening hyperemesis gravidarum unresponsive to con- ventional treatment,38 although a double-blind pilot study found it to be no more effective than promethazine.39 A systematic review found no evidence of benefit for any in- tervention in hyperemesis gravidarum.32 Radiotherapy. The risk of emesis with radiotherapy var- ies with the treatment given, particularly the area of the body irradiated. However, emetic risk, and recommenda- tions for use of antiemetics, are less clearly defined than in the situation of chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomit- ing.1 Use of a prophylactic 5-HT3 antagonist is usually rec- ommended in patients receiving radiation to the upper ab- domen. Dexamethasone may be added for those receiving total body irradiation.1,2 For radiotherapy of minimal eme- togenic potential, treatment on an as-needed only basis has been suggested.1 1.
